items.note: No cooldown time for the 2000 SBMD-3 XRCF test. Searched the UAH SBMD final report (NTRS 20010070993, snapshot eeebe569b2b068a9), the NASA Marshall Optics/XRCF page (868092de92113bdc) and the MSFC Optical Systems PDF (38d1495c6d2fd317): no time-to-temperature. A press figure of about five days per JWST segment cooldown exists, but it refers to the 2009+ JWST campaign after the 2005 helium-refrigeration upgrade, a different configuration, so it is not used.
The 1996 YBCO filter paper (NTRS 19970019925; record c41cdddf9f319825, full-text PDF 5591c682c8f78ebe) reports 77 K measurements but names no cryostat and gives no cooldown time.

The NIST NCNR Orange cryostat page (56791a020ab309b1) and BT-1 spec page (bd653acb7b6e2656) describe operation (10 L LHe reservoir, cold valve, pumping below 4.2 K) but give no cooldown time. ILL pages on Orange cryostats give only relative speed-ups (3x faster) and hold times, not a time-to-base for the NIST OC50.

The NIST project page (72975e149e80cf03) and NIST micro-JT papers (2009 development 9510c087a8ae4389; 2012 instability comparison 7f83202d82e52495; 2013 pulsating flow f7a7ea21aa1749fb) show cool-down curves or mention cool down but state no time to reach 77 K for this phase-II prototype.
The TriStar II Plus is held at 77 K by a passive liquid-nitrogen Dewar bath that the user fills. The instrument has no refrigerator and no cooldown stage, so there is no machine cooldown time.

The WARP paper (arXiv astro-ph/0701286, full text 26e764a0e4088978) says the container is cooled to about 86.5 K by an external liquid-argon bath and describes the initial filling, but gives no cooldown or filling duration.

The WSU HYPER CCC page (17a87d62bef4d9ee) gives 'Test Cycle Time (cryocooler on): ~ 6 hours per measurement'. That is a measurement cycle, not a time from room temperature to temperature, so it is not used. The Westra 2019 WSU thesis on this apparatus (ef9992038ae720bb) describes cooling to 180 K and about two hours per measurement step but gives no cooldown duration.

items.quote: 415 cryocooler takes approximately 4.5 hours to cool the test cell from room temperature to 20 K.
items.document_title: Mathew Hunt, Cryogenic Accelerated Fatigue Tester for Characterization (WSU M.S. thesis, 2021)
items.location: Section 4.3.2 Steady State Operation, thesis p. 81 (PDF page 94)
items.note: This is the builder's thesis for this exact CRAFT test cell. It reports the PT-415 cooling the cell from room temperature to 20 K. It is an approximate observed figure, not a vendor spec. Evacuation before cooldown (2-3 h roughing) and warm-up (14-16 h) are separate and are not included.

The cryoSPHERE IFU (66423dd6da29391c) gives operating range -50 to -70 C, a 30-second Pre-Freeze priming cycle and a default 120 s ablation timer. It does not state a time for the probe to reach operating temperature. The 30 s priming setting is a procedure step, not a documented cooldown time, so it is not used.

EPA SOP 5188 (f580c75f9b830d13) gives the LN2-cooled trap setpoints only in a screenshot, a 10 min bakeout, and 2 h / >12 h air-water check times after pump-down. None is a time for the trap to cool to its -180 C precool temperature.

ESPEC Global-N brochures (268cee2caaa75e55, 7559539b49137986, 5841b3cd5a2f94a8, 15845c60301db18c) and the model page (0203b7ff347a91e8) give only an average cooling rate for EGNX12-4NWL (6 C/m, 180 to -70 C per IEC 60068-3-5 at supply air). They give no pull-down time from room temperature to a set point. Deriving one from the rate would be an estimate.

Cryotop vitrification uses a user-filled liquid-nitrogen container and plunging. There is no refrigerated machine and no cooldown stage. The protocol's timed steps (ES/VS equilibration minutes) are part of the run, not a cooldown.
